name: CLAT UG
fullName: Common Law Admission Test – Undergraduate (5-year integrated LL.B.)
eligibility: 10+2 with 45% (40% for SC/ST); candidates appearing in Class 12 in March/April 2027 may apply; no upper age limit

notification.summary: The Consortium of NLUs notified CLAT 2027 on 22 Jul 2026. Online applications opened on 3 Aug 2026 and are open until 31 Oct 2026; the pen-and-paper exam is on Sunday 6 Dec 2026 (2–4 pm). The Consortium has said the syllabus and pattern are unchanged. Checked via web search on 2026-10-10 (news/coaching reports citing consortiumofnlus.ac.in).

pattern.notes: Officially the section ranges are English 22–26, Current Affairs 28–32, Legal 28–32, Logical 22–26 and Quantitative 10–14 questions; the mock uses mid-range values. Every section is passage/caselet based: English passages of about 450 words with 5–6 questions each; Current Affairs news passages with about 5 questions that often go beyond the passage to related static facts; Legal passages stating a principle, statute or judgment followed by 5–6 fact situations; Logical Reasoning argument passages with 5–6 critical-reasoning questions (plus an occasional analytical puzzle set); Quantitative caselets or tables with about 5 questions. Questions linked to a shared passage are always served together as a set; some older items still carry their own short stimulus. No sectional time limit.

trendAnalysis.summary: Since CLAT 2024 the paper has 120 questions in 120 minutes (down from 150), all passage-based. Legal Reasoning and Current Affairs carry the most weight (≈25% each); legal passages increasingly draw on recent statutes and judgments (BNS/BNSS, data protection, constitutional cases), but answers still follow strictly from the principle stated. Current Affairs passages cover the 12–15 months before the exam, with questions frequently testing related static facts (constitutional articles, institutions, treaties). English passages are long but moderate; Logical Reasoning focuses on argument analysis rather than puzzles; Quant is class-10 arithmetic in caselet form. CLAT 2026 (Dec 2025) was rated moderate overall, with lengthy legal passages and a time-consuming quant section.

pyqBlueprint.method: Compiled from the Consortium of NLUs' published question papers and answer keys for CLAT 2024, CLAT 2025 and CLAT 2026 (held 3 Dec 2023, 1 Dec 2024 and 7 Dec 2025) as summarised in post-exam analyses (IMS, Hitbullseye, LegalEdge, CLAT NLTI) found via web search; the full papers could not be fetched in this session, so section-wise question types were consolidated from those analyses and the writer's own knowledge. Notable 2026 shift: Logical Reasoning carried more analytical/arithmetical items (puzzles, blood relations, directions) alongside critical-reasoning passages. All patterns are paraphrased; no actual question or passage is reproduced.

archetypes.pattern: Op-ed style passage (≈450 words) on a public-policy or legal theme; 'main idea / central argument' with distractors that are partial, extreme or contrary
Best summary or most appropriate title for the passage; wrong titles are too narrow (one example) or too broad/extreme
What can be inferred from the passage or from a specific statement/example in it; distractors overreach or contradict
What the author would agree with / what a character's remark implies; tests reading of stance rather than literal detail
Meaning of a word as used in the passage; distractors include the word's other (literal or unrelated) senses
Meaning of an idiom or figurative phrase used in the passage
Tone/attitude of the author, options pairing close adjectives (concerned vs indignant, ironic vs mournful)
Primary purpose of the passage or a paragraph (to propose, critique, compare, examine both sides)
Fill-in or correct-usage item set inside a passage sentence: subject–verb agreement with 'along with/neither…nor', tense

Principle of negligence (duty, breach, foreseeability) applied to facts where the defendant took reasonable care or the plaintiff's own conduct caused harm
Strict/absolute liability and defences (volenti, act of God, rescue doctrine) applied to a fact situation
Vicarious liability: was the employee acting in the course of employment or on a 'frolic of his own'?
Offer/acceptance and communication rules (postal acceptance, revocation timing, silence)
Consideration, capacity (minor's agreement void ab initio) and free consent applied to facts

passages.title: Passage I
passages.text:
There is a particular kind of afternoon that my generation remembers and our children may never know. It began after lunch, somewhere around the third hour of a school holiday, when every comic had been read and every cousin had gone home. Nothing happened, and nothing was expected to happen. We complained about it bitterly. Then, almost always, something did happen: a cardboard box became a ship, a notebook filled up with the laws of an invented country, a younger brother was persuaded to star in a play in which he was, for reasons never explained, a tiger.

I have been thinking about those afternoons because they seem to be disappearing. A child today who reaches the edge of boredom has an exit within arm's length. The phone does not merely fill the empty hour; it abolishes it. Every lull is now a gap in a feed, and the feed has been engineered by some of the best-paid minds on the planet to make sure the gap closes before anything else can grow in it.

It is tempting to treat this as a problem of willpower — to tell parents to be firmer and children to be stronger. But that framing lets the design off the hook. When a product is built to be difficult to put down, asking a twelve-year-old to put it down is a little like asking a swimmer to ignore the current. Some will manage. Many will not, and the ones who fail will be told that the failure is theirs.

Nor am I persuaded by the opposite reflex, which is to ban the devices outright and hope the old afternoons return. Several governments have recently moved to restrict children's access to social media, and their instinct is understandable. Yet prohibition tends to treat the screen as the disease rather than the symptom. The deeper loss is not of time away from devices but of time that is unclaimed — time that no one, not a parent, not a teacher, not an app, has already decided how to fill.

Boredom, in this sense, is less an absence than a threshold. It is the discomfort a mind feels just before it is forced to supply its own entertainment, and that act of supplying is where imagination is exercised. A child who never crosses the threshold is not necessarily less intelligent or less happy. But she may be less practised at a skill that adulthood will demand of her constantly: sitting with an unstructured problem until it yields.

What would it mean to protect that threshold? Probably something duller than a law. Schools that build in breaks without organised activities. Families that keep one room, or one hour, deliberately empty. Designers who are required, at the very least, to stop optimising for the elimination of the pause. None of this will bring back the cardboard ship. But it might leave enough room for a child to build a different one.

passages.title: Passage II
passages.text:
On his last morning at the district court, Haridas Menon arrived, as he had for thirty-one years, eleven minutes before anyone else. He unlocked the steel cupboard, took out the stenograph machine he had bought with his own money in 1994, and set it on the little desk below the judge's dais. Then he remembered, and put it back.

The new system had been installed over the summer. Three microphones hung from the ceiling like patient spiders, and a screen beside the witness box displayed, in grey letters, whatever anyone said, a second or two after they said it. The young registrar had explained that the software had been trained on thousands of hours of courtroom speech. 'It even understands Malayalam-English, sir,' she had said, as if that would console him.

It did understand, mostly. Haridas had watched it for a week. It caught the advocates' long sentences and the judge's dry asides. It did not catch the witness who said 'yes' while shaking her head, or the long pause before a policeman answered a question about the time of an arrest. Those things had never been in the transcript either, strictly speaking. But Haridas had known where they were. He had marked them in his own shorthand in the margin — a small circle for a hesitation, a slanting line for a contradiction — and more than one judge, reading his notes late at night before writing a judgment, had sent for him to ask what a circle meant.

At eleven, Justice Lakshmi Varier, who was hearing a land dispute, paused the proceedings. 'Before we go on,' she said, 'I understand this is Mr. Menon's last day.' The advocates turned. Haridas, who had spent three decades being the one person in the room no one looked at, found that he did not know where to put his hands.

'For many years,' the judge continued, 'I have relied on records I could trust because a person I could trust prepared them. I hope the machine will be as accurate. I am less sure it will be as attentive.' She smiled. 'The two are not the same thing, though we often confuse them.'

The screen dutifully printed her words. Haridas noticed that it had spelt 'attentive' correctly, and that it had left out the smile.

In the afternoon the registrar brought him a cake and a printed certificate. He thanked her, and meant it. On the bus home he took out a pocket diary and, out of habit, began to note down the conversation of two college students in the seat ahead — their quarrel, and the place where one of them nearly apologised and did not. Halfway down the page he stopped, looked at what he had written, and drew a small circle in the margin.

passages.title: Passage III
passages.text:
In most Indian cities, you can tell a neighbourhood's income by looking up. Where the money is, the sky is broken by trees — rain trees and gulmohars planted a generation ago along wide avenues, their canopies meeting over the road. Where it is not, the sky is a flat white glare, interrupted only by tangled cables and the occasional tin roof that ticks as it expands in the afternoon heat.

The difference is not merely aesthetic. Studies of urban heat repeatedly find that surface temperatures in densely built, treeless settlements can run several degrees higher than in leafy districts a short drive away. During a heatwave, those degrees are the difference between a hard day and a dangerous one. The people who live in the hottest neighbourhoods are also the people least able to escape them: they work outdoors, they sleep in rooms without cooling, and their homes are built of materials that store heat by day and release it by night.

Cities have begun to respond. Several now publish heat action plans, which issue warnings, open cooling shelters and shift working hours during extreme temperatures. These measures save lives, and they deserve credit. But they are designed for emergencies, and heat in a warming country is ceasing to be an emergency. It is becoming a climate in the literal sense — a condition one lives in rather than an event one survives.

That shift demands a different kind of planning. A heat plan treats the hot neighbourhood as a place to be rescued from; long-term policy must treat it as a place to be repaired. That means trees, but not only trees, since a sapling planted this monsoon will take a decade to cast useful shade. It means reflective roofing, which can be applied in weeks; building codes that require ventilation in low-cost housing; and the protection of the small water bodies that cities have spent half a century filling in.

None of this is technically difficult. The obstacle is that shade, unlike a flyover, has no ribbon to cut. Its benefits are diffuse, slow and invisible — they show up as illnesses that did not happen and working days that were not lost. A municipal budget that rewards visible construction will always find shade a hard sell.

There is, however, a way to make the invisible visible. If cities measured and published neighbourhood temperatures with the same regularity as they publish air-quality readings, the gap between the leafy avenue and the treeless settlement would become a number that councillors could be asked about. What is counted tends to be cared for. The heat has always been measured by the people who live in it; it is time it was measured by the people who govern them.

passages.title: Passage IV
passages.text:
A law that the people it governs cannot read is a strange kind of law. It binds them, but it does not speak to them. Most citizens encounter legislation only second-hand — through a lawyer, a news report or a notice pinned to a government office wall — and by the time it reaches them it has passed through so many interpreters that its original wording hardly seems to matter. Or so it is commonly assumed.

The assumption is convenient for drafters, and it has shaped the way statutes are written. Sentences run to a hundred words. Provisos qualify provisos. Definitions sit in one section, exceptions in another and the operative rule in a third, so that understanding a single obligation requires holding three pages open at once. Lawyers defend this style as precision: ordinary language, they argue, is too loose to bear the weight of rights and penalties, and every apparently redundant phrase is there because some past litigant exploited its absence.

There is truth in this. Legal drafting is not creative writing, and a statute that charms its readers but leaves a loophole has failed at its main task. But the defence proves less than it claims. Much legal obscurity is not the residue of hard-won precision; it is habit, inherited from drafters who wrote for other lawyers because no one else was expected to read. 'Notwithstanding anything hereinbefore contained' rarely does work that 'despite section 4' could not.

Several jurisdictions have shown that clarity and precision are not enemies. Statutes have been redrafted with shorter sentences, worked examples and explanatory notes, without any measurable rise in litigation. Indian legislation has occasionally done the same: the illustrations attached to provisions of the criminal law have, for more than a century, shown readers how an abstract rule applies to concrete facts, and courts have generally found them helpful rather than distracting.

The stakes are not merely stylistic. When the law is opaque, the advantage goes to those who can afford to have it explained. A tenant who cannot read her lease, or a small trader who cannot follow a tax notice, is not merely inconvenienced; she is placed at the mercy of whoever can. Clarity, in this sense, is a question of equality before the law, not of elegance.

None of this means that every citizen should be expected to read every statute. It means that those who wish to should be able to — and that drafters should write as if someone outside the profession were looking over their shoulder. Sooner or later, someone always is.

passages.title: Passage I
passages.text:
The results of the Assembly elections to four States and one Union Territory, declared on 4 May 2026, redrew the political map of eastern and southern India. In West Bengal, the Bharatiya Janata Party won 207 of the 294 seats, ending roughly fifteen years of Trinamool Congress rule. Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee lost her own constituency, Bhabanipur, to Suvendu Adhikari, who on 9 May was sworn in at Kolkata's Brigade Parade Ground as the State's first BJP Chief Minister.

In Tamil Nadu, the actor-politician C. Joseph Vijay, whose party, the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK), was contesting its first Assembly election, won 108 seats in the 234-member House — short of the majority mark of 118. With the support of the Congress, the Left parties and others, Vijay was sworn in on 10 May, becoming the first Chief Minister since 1967 who belongs to neither the DMK nor the AIADMK. The Governor directed him to prove his majority on the floor of the House within days of taking office.

In Kerala, the Congress-led United Democratic Front won 102 of the 140 seats, and V. D. Satheesan was sworn in as Chief Minister on 18 May, returning the UDF to power after a decade. The BJP-led alliance retained power in Assam for a third consecutive term, and the NDA also held Puducherry.

The verdicts were striking for more than their margins. The BJP had never before formed a government in West Bengal, and in Tamil Nadu the two Dravidian parties had taken turns in power for nearly six decades. In Kerala, the outgoing Left Democratic Front government had in 2021 become the first in the State's history to win a second consecutive term; this time the State returned to its older pattern of alternating between the two fronts.

For most of these States, the polls were the first held after the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls, carried out in the preceding winter.

passages.title: Passage II
passages.text:
On 12 August 2026, the Rajya Sabha passed by voice vote the Kerala (Alteration of Name) Bill, 2026, a day after the Lok Sabha had approved it. The Bill changes the name of the State of Kerala to 'Keralam' — the name by which the State has long been known in Malayalam — by amending the relevant entry in the First Schedule to the Constitution. The Kerala Legislative Assembly had unanimously adopted a resolution in 2024 urging the Union Government to make the change. In Malayalam the State has always been called 'Keralam', and its formation is celebrated every year on 1 November as Kerala Piravi.

Following the procedure laid down in the Constitution, the President referred the draft Bill to the State Legislature for its views before it was introduced in Parliament, and the Union Cabinet cleared the proposal in February 2026. The Bill also empowers the appropriate government, for one year, to adapt existing laws so that references to 'Kerala' are read as references to 'Keralam', and provides that pending proceedings will continue under the new name.

The State itself came into being on 1 November 1956, when Malayalam-speaking areas of the former Travancore-Cochin State were joined with the Malabar district of Madras State under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956. It is not the first State to change its name since then; several others have done so through laws enacted by Parliament in the same way.

passages.title: Passage IV
passages.text:
On 15 July 2026, the India–United Kingdom Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) entered into force, almost a year after it was signed in London in July 2025 in the presence of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer. A companion Double Contribution Convention took effect on the same day. Under the agreement, the bulk of India's exports gain duty-free access to the British market, while India phases down its tariffs on items such as British cars and whisky over several years.

The CETA is the second agreement with a European partner to take effect in less than a year. The Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement (TEPA) with the four-nation European Free Trade Association, signed in March 2024, entered into force on 1 October 2025; it is notable for a commitment by the EFTA States to promote investment of USD 100 billion in India over fifteen years. Negotiations with the European Union, first launched in 2007 and revived in 2022, were concluded at the India–EU Summit in New Delhi on 27 January 2026, though that agreement must still be signed and ratified before it can take effect.

The agreements come as India seeks to diversify its export markets amid rising tariffs elsewhere, and as the multilateral trading system under the World Trade Organization struggles to conclude new agreements. They build on India's earlier pacts with the United Arab Emirates and Australia, both of which came into force in 2022, and mark a shift from the caution India showed after it stayed out of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership in 2019.

passages.title: Passage I
passages.text:
Section 10 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 provides that an agreement is a contract if it is made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object. Under Section 14, consent is 'free' when it is not caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation or mistake.

Coercion (Section 15) is the committing, or threatening to commit, any act forbidden by the Indian Penal Code (now the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023), or the unlawful detaining, or threatening to detain, any property, to the prejudice of any person whatever, with the intention of causing any person to enter into an agreement. It is immaterial whether the coercion is employed by a party to the contract or by a stranger, and whether it is directed at the contracting party or at someone else.

Undue influence (Section 16) exists where the relations between the parties are such that one of them is in a position to dominate the will of the other and uses that position to obtain an unfair advantage over the other. A person is deemed to be in such a position where he holds real or apparent authority over the other, stands in a fiduciary relation to the other, or makes a contract with a person whose mental capacity is temporarily or permanently affected by reason of age, illness or mental or bodily distress. Where such a person enters into a transaction that appears, on the face of it, to be unconscionable, the burden of proving that it was not induced by undue influence lies upon the person in a position to dominate the will of the other.

Fraud (Section 17) includes the suggestion, as a fact, of that which is not true by one who does not believe it to be true; the active concealment of a fact by one having knowledge of it; and a promise made without any intention of performing it — when done by a party to the contract with intent to deceive the other party or to induce him to enter into the contract. Mere silence as to facts likely to affect a person's willingness to enter into a contract is not fraud, unless the circumstances are such that the person keeping silence has a duty to speak, or unless his silence is, in itself, equivalent to speech.

Misrepresentation (Section 18) includes the positive assertion, in a manner not warranted by the information of the person making it, of that which is not true, though he believes it to be true.

When consent is caused by coercion, fraud or misrepresentation, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused (Section 19). But if consent was caused by misrepresentation, or by silence that is fraudulent within the meaning of Section 17, the contract is not voidable if the party whose consent was so caused had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence. A fraud or misrepresentation that did not cause the consent of the party does not render the contract voidable. A contract induced by undue influence is likewise voidable (Section 19A), and the court may set it aside absolutely or on such terms as it thinks just.

passages.title: Passage II
passages.text:
Negligence, as a tort, has three elements: the defendant owed the plaintiff a duty of care; the defendant breached that duty by failing to take the care that a reasonable person would have taken in the circumstances; and the breach caused the plaintiff damage of a kind that was not too remote. Without damage, there is no actionable negligence, however careless the defendant may have been.

The standard of care is objective and impersonal. A defendant's inexperience or lack of ability is not taken into account; he is judged by what a reasonable and competent person undertaking that activity would have done. The degree of care required rises with the likelihood of harm and the seriousness of the harm that may result, and is weighed against the cost and practicability of precautions. A person is not required to guard against a risk so small that a reasonable person, considering it, would think it right to disregard it.

Where the defendant professes a special skill, such as a doctor, an electrician or an architect, he is judged by the standard of an ordinary competent member of that profession. Following Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab (2005), a professional is not negligent merely because a better alternative course or method was available, or because another professional would have acted differently, so long as he acted in accordance with a practice accepted as proper by a reasonable body of professionals in that field at that time. A mere error of judgment, or an accident, is not in itself proof of negligence.

The plaintiff must ordinarily prove negligence. However, under the maxim res ipsa loquitur ('the thing speaks for itself'), negligence may be inferred where the thing that caused the harm was under the management and control of the defendant or his servants, and the accident is of a kind that does not ordinarily happen if those in control use proper care. The defendant may then rebut the inference by showing how the accident happened without negligence on his part.

Where the plaintiff's own failure to take reasonable care for his own safety contributes to the damage he suffers, he is guilty of contributory negligence. In India, contributory negligence does not defeat the claim; the damages are reduced in proportion to the plaintiff's share of responsibility for the damage.

passages.title: Passage III
passages.text:
The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), which replaced the Indian Penal Code with effect from 1 July 2024, retains the traditional offences against property and adds a new one.

Theft (Section 303): Whoever, intending to take dishonestly any movable property out of the possession of any person without that person's consent, moves that property in order to such taking, is said to commit theft. A person acts 'dishonestly' if he acts with the intention of causing wrongful gain to one person or wrongful loss to another. The taking need not be permanent, and a person may commit theft even of property that belongs to him, if he dishonestly takes it out of the possession of another person who lawfully holds it.

Snatching (Section 304): Theft is snatching if, in order to commit theft, the offender suddenly or quickly or forcibly seizes or secures or grabs or takes away from any person or from his possession any movable property.

Extortion (Section 308): Whoever intentionally puts any person in fear of any injury to that person, or to any other, and thereby dishonestly induces the person so put in fear to deliver to any person any property or valuable security, commits extortion. In extortion the victim's consent to part with the property is obtained by fear; in theft the property is taken without consent.

Robbery (Section 309): In all robbery there is either theft or extortion. Theft is robbery if, in order to the committing of the theft, or in committing the theft, or in carrying away or attempting to carry away property obtained by the theft, the offender, for that end, voluntarily causes or attempts to cause to any person death or hurt or wrongful restraint, or fear of instant death or of instant hurt or of instant wrongful restraint. Extortion is robbery if the offender, at the time of committing the extortion, is in the presence of the person put in fear, and commits the extortion by putting that person in fear of instant death, of instant hurt or of instant wrongful restraint to that person or to some other person, and, by so putting in fear, induces the person so put in fear then and there to deliver up the thing extorted.

Dacoity (Section 310): When five or more persons conjointly commit or attempt to commit a robbery, or where the whole number of persons conjointly committing or attempting to commit a robbery, and persons present and aiding such commission or attempt, amount to five or more, every person so committing, attempting or aiding is said to commit dacoity.

passages.title: Passage IV
passages.text:
Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, nothing is an offence which is done in the exercise of the right of private defence (Section 34). Every person has a right to defend his own body, and the body of any other person, against any offence affecting the human body; and his own or any other person's property, movable or immovable, against theft, robbery, mischief or criminal trespass, or an attempt to commit any of them (Section 35).

The right is available even against an act that would otherwise be an offence but is not one because the person doing it is a child, of unsound mind, or intoxicated, or is acting under a misconception (Section 36).

The right is subject to limits (Section 37). There is no right of private defence in cases in which there is time to have recourse to the protection of the public authorities. And the right in no case extends to the inflicting of more harm than it is necessary to inflict for the purpose of defence.

The right of private defence of the body extends to voluntarily causing death only if the offence that occasions its exercise is of a grave kind, such as an assault that reasonably causes the apprehension that death or grievous hurt will otherwise be the consequence, an assault with the intention of committing rape or of kidnapping or abducting, or an act of throwing or administering acid, or an attempt to do so, that reasonably causes the apprehension that grievous hurt will otherwise be the consequence (Section 38). In other cases the right extends only to causing harm other than death (Section 39).

The right of private defence of the body commences as soon as a reasonable apprehension of danger to the body arises from an attempt or threat to commit the offence, though the offence may not have been committed, and it continues as long as such apprehension continues (Section 40). It is a right of defence, not of retaliation or punishment; when the danger ends, the right ends with it.

Courts have repeatedly held that the force used in private defence is not to be weighed 'in golden scales'. A person facing sudden danger cannot be expected to calculate precisely how much force is needed; the question is whether the force used was reasonable in the circumstances as they reasonably appeared to him at the time.

passages.title: Passage V
passages.text:
Article 14 of the Constitution provides that the State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India. Equality does not mean that every law must apply identically to everyone; the State may treat different classes of persons differently. But the classification must be reasonable.

Since State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar (1952), the Supreme Court has applied a two-part test to a classification. First, it must be founded on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes the persons or things grouped together from those left out of the group. Second, the differentia must have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the law. A classification need not be mathematically perfect, and the legislature is presumed to understand the needs of its own people; but a classification that is arbitrary, or that singles out a person or group for hostile treatment without any rational basis, will fail. The object of the law must itself be lawful: a classification cannot be saved by showing that it is rationally connected to an object that is itself discriminatory.

From E. P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974) onwards, the Court has also held that equality is antithetical to arbitrariness. In Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017), it held that legislation, and not merely executive action, may be struck down if it is 'manifestly arbitrary' — that is, if it is capricious or irrational, made without an adequate determining principle, or excessive and disproportionate.

Article 14 protects 'any person', and so extends to non-citizens and to companies. It does not, however, prevent the State from making special provisions for groups that the Constitution itself identifies, such as women and children under Article 15(3).

passages.title: Passage I
passages.text:
The city council's transport committee has proposed that all municipal bus services be made free of charge from next April. Supporters point to several European towns that abolished fares and reported a sharp rise in ridership within a year. The committee's chair argues that because a bus carries in the road space of two or three cars as many people as forty cars would, every new bus passenger represents one car fewer on the road, and that free fares will therefore ease the congestion that costs the city's economy hundreds of crores of rupees a year. The loss of fare revenue, she adds, is small: fares currently cover only about a quarter of the bus service's operating cost, and the rest is already met from the city budget.

Critics are unconvinced. They note that in some towns that abolished fares, much of the new ridership came from people who had previously walked or cycled short distances, not from drivers. They also point out that the city's buses are already overcrowded at peak hours, so that a surge in passengers could make the service less attractive to exactly the commuters the council hopes to lure out of their cars. In their view, the money would be better spent on more frequent services and dedicated bus lanes, since surveys of car owners in the city most often cite unreliability and slow journeys — not fares — as their reasons for not taking the bus.

passages.title: Passage II
passages.text:
A State has made pre-institution mediation compulsory for all commercial disputes valued below ₹1 crore: before filing a suit, a party must first attempt mediation at a legal services centre. Two years on, the State's law department has published figures showing that the number of such commercial suits filed in its courts has fallen by 40%. The department's report concludes that compulsory mediation is resolving disputes that would otherwise have clogged the courts, and recommends extending the requirement to commercial disputes of every value.

The report also notes that only about a third of the disputes sent to mediation ended in a settlement; in the rest, the parties were issued a certificate stating that mediation had failed, and became free to sue.

A senior advocate, writing in a legal journal, argued that the figures are being read too generously. She pointed out that during the same two years the court fees for commercial suits in the State were doubled, and that a new online grievance portal diverted many small business disputes away from the civil courts. She added that in high-value disputes the parties are usually represented by lawyers who have already explored settlement before going to court, so that compulsory mediation in such cases is likely to add delay without adding settlements.

passages.title: Passage III
passages.text:
Over the past decade, the number of tigers counted in a national park rose from 48 to 71. The park's director attributes the increase to a programme, begun at the start of the decade, that relocated three villages from the park's core zone to new settlements outside it, compensating each family generously. 'Remove people from the core,' he wrote in his annual report, 'and the tigers will return. Every tiger reserve in the country should follow our model.' He adds that forest guards now routinely sight tigers in the former village areas, and that cattle grazing, which once competed with the deer and sambar on which tigers prey, has ended in the core.

A wildlife biologist who has studied the park disputes this reading. She notes that midway through the decade the counting method changed from tracing pugmarks to camera traps, which detect animals more reliably. She also observes that a neighbouring park, which relocated no villages, recorded a similar rise in tiger numbers over the same period. And she points out that the relocated villagers had depended on the forest for grazing, firewood and minor forest produce; their removal, she says, may well have helped tigers, but at a cost to communities that the director's report does not count.

passages.title: Passage IV
passages.text:
Restaurants rated 4.5 stars or more on the city's most popular food-delivery app receive, on average, three times as many orders as restaurants rated between 3.5 and 4.4. A consultancy that advises restaurant owners has concluded from this that a high rating causes higher sales, and it now offers, for a monthly fee, to 'manage' a client's online reputation by encouraging satisfied customers to post reviews and by responding promptly to complaints. It cites a client whose rating rose from 4.2 to 4.6 within six months of signing up, and whose orders doubled over the same period.

Some restaurant owners have their doubts. One notes that the app places highly rated restaurants at the top of its search results, so that a rating may influence sales chiefly through visibility rather than through customers' judgment of quality. A food critic adds a different concern: if every restaurant pays to manage its reputation, ratings will rise across the board and will cease to distinguish good kitchens from bad ones — leaving customers no better informed and restaurants no better off, while the consultancy collects its fees.

passages.title: Passage V (Analytical Reasoning)
passages.text:
A district court must hear six bail applications — P, Q, R, S, T and U — on six consecutive working days from Monday to Saturday of the same week, one application per day. The listing must satisfy the following conditions:

1. Q is heard on an earlier day than S, and exactly two applications are heard between Q and S.
2. P is heard either on Wednesday or on Thursday.
3. T is heard on the day immediately after R.
4. U is heard neither on Monday nor on Saturday.

passages.title: Caselet I
passages.text:
A National Law University received 12,000 applications for its five-year integrated programme in 2026. Women made up 45% of the applicants. Of the women applicants, 20% were domiciled in the State in which the university is located; of the men applicants, 25% were so domiciled.

The university admitted 180 students in all. Of these, 60 were admitted against domicile seats — 35 women and 25 men — and the remaining 120 against non-domicile seats, of whom 54 were women. (Every student admitted against a domicile seat is a domiciled applicant, and every student admitted against a non-domicile seat is a non-domiciled applicant.)

passages.text:
The table shows the work of the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions of four districts in 2025. The number pending at the end of the year equals pending at start + filed − disposed.

District | Pending at start | Filed | Disposed

passages.title: Caselet III
passages.text:
Asha and Bilal start a stationery business on 1 April 2025. Asha invests ₹3,00,000 at the start. Bilal invests ₹2,00,000 at the start and a further ₹1,00,000 on 1 October 2025. Their agreement provides that Bilal, who runs the shop, is first paid a salary of ₹4,000 a month, and the remaining profit is shared in the ratio of capital multiplied by the time for which it was invested.

The shop's best-selling item is a laser printer, bought at ₹8,000. The shop marks it up by 40% and normally sells it at a discount of 15% on the marked price.

questions.question:
Principle: An employer is vicariously liable for a wrong committed by an employee in the course of employment, that is, while doing the work he was employed to do, even if done in an unauthorised manner. The employer is not liable for acts done by the employee on a 'frolic of his own', unconnected with his employment.

Facts: Sunil, a delivery driver for QuickMart, is told to drive only on main roads. To save time while delivering a parcel, he takes a narrow lane and negligently knocks down a pedestrian, Kavya.

Is QuickMart liable to Kavya?
options: Yes, because Sunil was doing his job of delivering, though in an unauthorised manner.
No, because Sunil was on a frolic of his own.
Yes, but only if QuickMart owned the lane.
No, because Sunil disobeyed the instruction to use main roads.
questions.explanation: Sunil was delivering a parcel — the very work he was employed to do — only by a forbidden route. That is an unauthorised manner of doing authorised work, not a frolic of his own, so QuickMart is vicariously liable.

relevance.note: Unauthorised manner vs frolic on delivery driver; classic CLAT vicarious liability trap (option 3)

questions.question:
Principle: Whoever intentionally takes dishonestly any movable property out of the possession of any person without that person's consent, moving that property in order to such taking, commits theft. 'Dishonestly' means with the intention of causing wrongful gain to one person or wrongful loss to another.

Facts: Neha borrows her friend Ritu's bicycle with Ritu's permission for an afternoon. In the evening, instead of returning it, Neha sells it and keeps the money.

Has Neha committed theft?
options: No, because a bicycle is not movable property.
Yes, because she caused wrongful loss to Ritu.
No, because the bicycle was not taken out of Ritu's possession without her consent.
Yes, because she sold the bicycle dishonestly.
questions.explanation: Theft requires taking out of another's possession without consent. Neha obtained possession with Ritu's consent; her later dishonest sale may be another offence (such as criminal breach of trust or misappropriation), but on the stated principle it is not theft.

relevance.note: Entrusted bicycle sold: no taking out of possession, so not theft; dishonesty distractors are the real CLAT trap

questions.question:
Principle: Article 20(1): No person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law in force at the time of the commission of the act charged as an offence, nor be subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of the commission of the offence.

Facts: In January, Deepak sold loose cigarettes near a school, which was then punishable with a fine of ₹200. In March, the law was amended to raise the fine to ₹2,000. In April, Deepak was convicted for the January sale.

What is the maximum fine that can lawfully be imposed on Deepak?
options: No fine, because the law was amended
questions.explanation: Article 20(1) bars a penalty greater than that under the law in force when the offence was committed. In January the fine was ₹200, so that is the maximum; the act was an offence at the time, so he can still be punished.

relevance.note: Art 20(1) heavier penalty bar: fine capped at Rs 200; neat CLAT constitutional application

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"After the town installed CCTV cameras in its market, reported thefts in the market fell by 30% within a year. The council concludes that the cameras deterred thieves."

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the council's conclusion?
options: Thefts in neighbouring streets without cameras rose during the year.
The council spent a large sum on installing the cameras.
Many shopkeepers support the use of cameras.
Reported thefts in comparable markets without cameras did not fall over the same period.
questions.explanation: A control comparison showing no decline elsewhere rules out a general trend as the cause. A rise in neighbouring streets suggests displacement rather than deterrence; cost and opinion are irrelevant.

relevance.note: Control-group strengthener vs displacement option 0 as subtle trap; good CLAT CR
