questions.question:
Read the principle and facts and answer the question.

Principle: A person is liable in negligence if he owes a duty of care to another, breaches that duty by failing to take the care a reasonable person would take in the circumstances, and the breach causes foreseeable harm. A person who has taken all reasonable precautions is not liable.

Facts: A supermarket mops one aisle during business hours and places two large, brightly coloured 'Wet Floor' boards at either end of the aisle. Raj, reading messages on his phone, walks past one board without looking up, slips and breaks his wrist.

Is the supermarket liable to Raj in negligence?
options: No, because it took the precautions a reasonable shop would take to warn customers of the wet floor.
Yes, because the floor should never be mopped during business hours.
No, because Raj was not a paying customer at the time of the fall.
Yes, because a shop owes a duty of care to every customer and Raj was injured on its premises.
questions.explanation: Duty exists, but there is no breach: clearly visible warning boards at both ends are reasonable precautions, and the principle excuses a defendant who took them. Injury on the premises alone does not establish negligence, and nothing suggests Raj was not a customer.

relevance.note: Wet-floor warnings = reasonable care; distractor 3 (duty alone) is the CLAT trap

questions.question:
Read the principle and facts and answer the question.

Principle: An employer is liable for a wrong committed by an employee in the course of employment, including an authorised act done in an unauthorised manner. The employer is not liable where the employee, at the time of the wrong, was acting purely for his own purposes, unconnected with his work (a 'frolic of his own').

Facts: Manoj drives a delivery van for SpeedCart. On a Sunday, when he is off duty, he takes the van from the depot without permission to drive his family to a wedding in another town, and negligently injures a cyclist, Farah.

Is SpeedCart liable to Farah?
options: No, because Manoj was using the van for his own purposes, unconnected with his work.
Yes, because Manoj is a SpeedCart employee and was driving its van.
Yes, because taking the van was an authorised act done in an unauthorised manner.
No, because Farah should have avoided the van.
questions.explanation: Manoj was off duty and drove without permission for a family trip—a frolic of his own, not the company's work. Ownership of the van and his status as an employee are not enough; there was no authorised act to perform.

relevance.note: Off-duty Sunday joyride is frolic; option 2 mirrors unauthorised-manner trap, good contrast

questions.question:
Read the principle and facts and answer the question.

Principle: A person who voluntarily consents to a known risk cannot claim damages for harm resulting from it (volenti non fit injuria). However, a person who takes a risk to rescue others from a danger created by the defendant's negligence is not treated as having consented to that risk.

Facts: Gopal negligently leaves his bullock cart unattended on a busy market street. The bullocks bolt towards a group of schoolchildren. Ravi, a shopkeeper, runs out and stops the animals, saving the children but suffering serious injuries.

Can Ravi recover damages from Gopal?
options: Yes, because a rescuer of people endangered by the defendant's negligence is not treated as consenting to the risk.
No, because Ravi knowingly and voluntarily exposed himself to the risk.
No, because Gopal did not intend the bullocks to bolt.
Yes, but only if one of the children was actually injured.
questions.explanation: The general volenti rule would bar a person who knowingly takes a risk, but the principle's exception covers rescuers facing a danger created by the defendant's negligence. Intention is irrelevant to negligence, and the children need not be harmed for the rescuer to recover.

relevance.note: Rescue doctrine (Haynes v Harwell) defeats volenti; option 1 is the natural trap

questions.question:
Read the principle and facts and answer the question.

Principle: Communication of an acceptance is complete as against the proposer when it is put in the course of transmission to him, so as to be out of the acceptor's power. A proposal may be revoked at any time before the communication of its acceptance is complete as against the proposer. Communication of a revocation is complete as against the person to whom it is made when it comes to his knowledge.

Facts: On 1 March, Asha posts a letter offering to sell her flat to Bilal for ₹60 lakh. Bilal receives it on 3 March and posts a letter of acceptance on 5 March. Asha had changed her mind and posted a letter of revocation on 4 March, which reaches Bilal on 6 March.

Is there a binding contract between Asha and Bilal?
options: Yes, because the acceptance was complete against Asha on 5 March, before her revocation reached Bilal on 6 March.
No, because Asha posted her revocation on 4 March, before Bilal posted his acceptance.
Yes, because an offer to sell immovable property cannot be revoked once made.
No, because Asha had not received Bilal's letter of acceptance when she revoked the offer.
questions.explanation: Revocation takes effect against Bilal only when it reaches him (6 March). Bilal's acceptance was complete against Asha when posted on 5 March, so the revocation came too late. Posting a revocation is not enough, and offers relating to property can be revoked in time.

relevance.note: Postal acceptance complete 5 Mar before revocation reaches 6 Mar; textbook CLAT ICA s.4/5 timeline trap

questions.question:
Read the principle and facts and answer the question.

Principle: When a contract is broken, the injured party may recover compensation for loss which naturally arose in the usual course of things from the breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach. No compensation is given for remote or indirect loss.

Facts: Harish, who runs a small flour mill, hands a broken crankshaft to TransFast couriers for delivery to a repair workshop, telling them only that it is 'machinery'. TransFast delivers it five days late. Harish had no spare crankshaft, so the mill stood idle throughout, and he lost ₹80,000 in profits. TransFast did not know this.

Can Harish recover the lost profits from TransFast?
options: No, because the crankshaft reached the workshop in the end.
Yes, because the late delivery was a breach of contract and the loss followed from it.
No, because TransFast did not know that the delay would stop the mill, so the loss of profits was not within the parties' contemplation.
Yes, because couriers are always liable for every consequence of delay.
questions.explanation: Mills often keep spares; a courier told only 'machinery' would not expect a delay to halt production. The lost profits neither arose in the usual course of things nor were known to be likely, so they are too remote. Breach alone does not make every loss recoverable.

relevance.note: Hadley v Baxendale crankshaft facts with remoteness; option 1 is the strong trap

questions.question:
Read the principle and facts and answer the question.

Principle: Whoever intentionally puts any person in fear of any injury to that person or to any other, and thereby dishonestly induces the person so put in fear to deliver any property to any person, commits extortion. 'Injury' includes any harm illegally caused to a person in body, mind, reputation or property.

Facts: Aman obtains private photographs of his former colleague Sneha and messages her that he will post them online unless she transfers ₹50,000 to his account. Frightened, Sneha transfers the money.

Has Aman committed extortion?
options: No, because Sneha transferred the money herself through her bank.
No, because Aman committed theft rather than extortion.
Yes, because he put Sneha in fear of injury to her reputation and thereby induced her to deliver money.
No, because he did not threaten Sneha with any physical harm.
questions.explanation: 'Injury' includes harm to reputation, so the threat suffices; the delivery of money induced by fear completes extortion. Delivery by the victim's own act is characteristic of extortion, which distinguishes it from theft.

relevance.note: Extortion via reputational threat; 'no physical harm' and 'bank transfer' distractors realistic

questions.question:
Read the principle and facts and answer the question.

Principle: Nothing is an offence which is done by a person who, by reason of a mistake of fact and not by reason of a mistake of law, in good faith believes himself to be justified by law in doing it.

Facts: The police circulate the photograph of an absconding murder accused. Sub-Inspector Rekha sees a man at a bus stand who closely resembles the photograph and, after comparing his face with it carefully, arrests him. The man turns out to be an innocent traveller.

Has Rekha committed an offence by arresting him?
options: No, because police officers can never be prosecuted for arrests.
Yes, because she arrested an innocent person.
Yes, because a mistake about a person's identity is a mistake of law.
No, because she acted in good faith under a mistake of fact, believing herself justified by law.
questions.explanation: Rekha's error concerned a fact (the man's identity), she checked carefully, and she believed the arrest was authorised by law—exactly the exception. Identity is a fact, not law; police officers are not immune in general.

relevance.note: Good-faith mistake of identity = mistake of fact; option 2 inverts law/fact, good trap

questions.question:
Read the principle and facts and answer the question.

Principle: When a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, each of them is liable for that act in the same manner as if it were done by him alone. A person is not liable under this rule for an act of another that was not in furtherance of the intention they shared.

Facts: Dinesh and Lalit plan to break into a shop at night, when they believe it will be empty, and steal cash. They agree that no one is to be harmed. Inside, a night watchman surprises them. Without any warning to Dinesh, Lalit pulls out a knife that Dinesh did not know he was carrying and fatally stabs the watchman. Dinesh flees.

Is Dinesh liable for the killing under the principle?
options: No, because the killing was not done in furtherance of the common intention, which was only to steal from an empty shop.
Yes, because every participant in a crime is liable for everything done during it.
No, because he ran away after the stabbing.
Yes, because he was present at the scene with Lalit.
questions.explanation: Their shared intention was theft without harm; Dinesh neither knew of the knife nor shared any intention to kill, so the stabbing was not in furtherance of the common intention. Presence alone is not enough, and fleeing afterwards is irrelevant to liability.

relevance.note: Common intention excludes unforeseen stabbing; mirrors CLAT s.34/BNS 3(5) problems

questions.question:
Read the principle and facts and answer the question.

Principle: Every citizen has the right to practise any profession or carry on any occupation, trade or business. The State may impose reasonable restrictions on this right in the interests of the general public. A restriction is unreasonable if it is excessive or disproportionate to the object it seeks to achieve, for instance where narrower measures would serve the purpose.

Facts: To ease congestion in three crowded markets in its capital, a State government issues an order permanently banning street vending everywhere in the State.

Is the order likely to be valid?
options: No, because the State can never restrict the right to carry on a trade.
Yes, because street vending is not a profession or business.
No, because a permanent State-wide ban is disproportionate to the aim of easing congestion in three markets.
Yes, because easing traffic congestion is in the interests of the general public.
questions.explanation: Public interest is a valid aim, but the measure goes far beyond it—banning vending everywhere, permanently, to solve a problem in three markets; narrower measures (vending zones, timings) would serve. Street vending is an occupation, and restrictions are allowed if reasonable.

relevance.note: State-wide permanent vending ban disproportionate; option 3 legitimate-aim trap

questions.question:
Read the principle and facts and answer the question.

Principle: No person accused of any offence shall be compelled to be a witness against himself. Courts have held that this protects an accused from being compelled to make testimonial statements based on personal knowledge, but not from being required to give physical evidence such as fingerprints, a specimen signature or a sample of handwriting.

Facts: In a forgery case, the magistrate directs the accused, Prakash, to give specimen samples of his handwriting so that they can be compared with the forged document. Prakash refuses, claiming that the order violates his right against self-incrimination.

Is Prakash's objection valid?
options: No, because giving a handwriting specimen is physical evidence, not a compelled testimonial statement.
Yes, because an accused can never be asked to provide anything to the court.
Yes, because the specimen may be used to prove him guilty.
No, because the right against self-incrimination does not apply in forgery cases.
questions.explanation: The principle limits protection to testimonial statements and expressly excludes handwriting samples. That the evidence may incriminate him does not convert it into testimony; the right applies to all offences.

relevance.note: Handwriting specimen not testimonial (Kathi Kalu Oghad); faithful Art 20(3) item

questions.question:
Read the principle and facts and answer the question.

Principle: Under the precautionary principle, where there are threats of serious or irreversible damage to the environment, lack of full scientific certainty shall not be used as a reason for postponing measures to prevent environmental degradation. The burden of proving that a proposed activity is environmentally benign lies on the person proposing it.

Facts: ChemCo applies to set up a chemical unit beside a wetland that hosts migratory birds. Expert studies on whether its effluents would harm the wetland are inconclusive. ChemCo argues that unless the State proves its unit will cause harm, permission cannot be refused.

Which of the following is correct?
options: The wetland can be protected only if the birds are an endangered species.
Permission must be granted until the studies become conclusive.
ChemCo's argument fails, because it must show that its unit is environmentally benign, and uncertainty does not favour it.
ChemCo's argument succeeds, because the State has not proved that harm will occur.
questions.explanation: The principle places the burden on the proponent and says scientific uncertainty is no reason to delay protection. So the State need not prove harm; inconclusive studies count against ChemCo. The principle has no endangered-species condition.

relevance.note: Precautionary principle with reversed burden (Vellore/Nayudu); option 3 is the trap

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"A coaching centre advertises: 'The average CLAT score of our students last year was 20 marks higher than the national average. Join us, and your score will rise too.'"

The advertisement assumes that:
options: the national average score will be the same this year
the centre has more teachers than its competitors
all students who join the centre study equally hard
the higher average score is due to the centre's coaching rather than to the centre admitting students who were already strong
questions.explanation: The claim that joining will raise your score holds only if coaching caused the gap; if the centre simply enrolled stronger students, the advertisement's conclusion collapses. The other options are not needed for the argument.

relevance.note: Coaching-ad selection-bias assumption; good CLAT CR with exam-related context

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"After the city banned thin plastic carry bags, the volume of plastic bags collected at its landfills fell by 40%. The municipal commissioner concluded that the ban has reduced the city's plastic waste."

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the commissioner's conclusion?
options: Cloth bags are more expensive than plastic carry bags.
Several other cities have also banned thin plastic carry bags.
Shopkeepers initially opposed the ban but later accepted it.
Since the ban, sales of thicker plastic garbage bags, which the ban does not cover, have risen sharply, and the total weight of plastic waste at the landfills has increased.
questions.explanation: The conclusion concerns total plastic waste, but the evidence counts only carry bags. If substitute plastic bags rose and total plastic waste by weight increased, the conclusion fails. The other options do not bear on the city's total plastic waste.

relevance.note: Bag ban weakened by substitution to thicker bags and total weight up; strong alternative-explanation item

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Researchers found that attendance rose by 15% in schools that introduced a free mid-day meal. They concluded that the meal programme increased school attendance."

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the researchers' conclusion?
options: The meals served in the programme met recommended nutritional standards.
In comparable nearby schools that did not introduce the meal during the same period, attendance remained unchanged.
Attendance in the schools had been falling for several years before the meal was introduced.
Parents said they liked the idea of a free meal for their children.
questions.explanation: A comparison group without the meal whose attendance stayed flat rules out a general rise (season, policy, economy) as the cause. Nutrition and parental approval do not show causation, and a prior falling trend does not by itself link the rise to the meal.

relevance.note: Control schools unchanged strengthens causal claim; option 2 (prior decline) is a smart trap

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

"Many of the country's most successful entrepreneurs dropped out of college. Therefore, students who want to build successful companies would improve their chances by dropping out."

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
options: College fees have risen sharply in the last decade.
Some successful entrepreneurs completed postgraduate degrees.
Several successful entrepreneurs later returned to complete their degrees.
Among all people who start companies, those who dropped out of college fail at a higher rate than graduates; the famous successes are a small fraction of dropouts.
questions.explanation: The argument looks only at successful dropouts. If dropouts as a group fail more often than graduates, dropping out does not improve one's chances. The other options are either consistent with the argument or irrelevant.

relevance.note: Dropout survivorship bias with base-rate weakener; classic CR done well

questions.question:
Read the information and answer the question.

A District Legal Services Authority received 2,400 applications for free legal aid in 2025. 40% of the applications came from women. 75% of the women's applications and 60% of the men's applications were approved.

Approximately what percentage of all approved applications came from women?
questions.explanation: Women: 960 applications, 720 approved. Men: 1,440 applications, 864 approved. Total approved = 1,584. Women's share = 720/1,584 ≈ 45.5%.

relevance.note: Approved share 720/1584 = 45.5% with 40/50 traps; CLAT legal-aid caselet style

questions.question:
Read the information and answer the question.

The table shows the number of cases filed and disposed of in four district courts in a year.

Court | Filed | Disposed
A | 1,200 | 900
B | 800 | 720
C | 1,500 | 1,050
D | 600 | 570

The combined disposal rate (cases disposed as a percentage of cases filed) of the four courts is closest to:
questions.explanation: Total disposed = 3,240; total filed = 4,100; 3,240/4,100 ≈ 79.0%. Averaging the four individual rates (75%, 90%, 70%, 95%) gives 82.5%, which is the trap.

relevance.note: Combined disposal 3240/4100 = 79% vs averaging percentages 82.5% trap; faithful

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the central argument of the passage?
options: Children today are less imaginative and less intelligent than earlier generations because smartphones have replaced boredom.
Governments should prohibit children's use of social media, because phones are deliberately engineered to be difficult to put down.
Children are losing unclaimed time in which imagination is exercised, and this is better addressed by protecting such time than by blaming individuals or simply banning devices.
Parents must exercise firmer control over their children's phone use if the creativity of earlier generations is to be restored.
questions.explanation: The author rejects both the 'willpower' framing (paragraph 3) and outright bans (paragraph 4), locates the real loss in 'unclaimed' time (paragraph 4–5) and ends with ways to protect it. The ban option is the view the author is 'not persuaded by'; the 'less intelligent' option contradicts 'not necessarily less intelligent'; the parental-control option is the framing the author says 'lets the design off the hook'.

relevance.note: CLAT-style main-idea on ~490w op-ed; distractors extreme (ban) and partial (parents); correct option somewhat longest

questions.question: The author would most likely agree with which of the following statements?
options: Organised after-school activities are the best way to fill the time children would otherwise spend on their phones.
A child's failure to put down a phone should not be treated chiefly as a personal failing, given how such products are designed.
Restrictions on children's social media use are misguided because they are driven by moral panic rather than evidence.
Children who rarely experience boredom are likely to grow up into unhappy adults.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the willpower framing 'lets the design off the hook' and that those who fail 'will be told that the failure is theirs' — the author disputes that. The author calls the instinct behind restrictions 'understandable', wants breaks 'without organised activities', and says such a child is 'not necessarily … less happy'.

relevance.note: Author-agrees item; 'moral panic' distractor nicely overreaches the 'understandable instinct' line

questions.question: As used in the passage ('The phone does not merely fill the empty hour; it abolishes it'), the word 'abolishes' most nearly means
options: does away with entirely
shortens considerably
formally outlaws
postpones to a later time
questions.explanation: The contrast 'does not merely fill … it abolishes' means the empty hour ceases to exist at all. 'Formally outlaws' is the word's legal sense, which does not fit an hour; 'shortens' and 'postpones' are weaker than the contrast requires.

relevance.note: Vocab-in-context with 'formally outlaws' literal-sense trap, as in CLAT; very easy

questions.question: The comparison of a twelve-year-old putting down a phone with 'asking a swimmer to ignore the current' is used to suggest that
options: children who do manage to resist their phones show exceptional discipline and deserve to be rewarded for it
physical activities such as swimming are the most effective way to draw children away from screens
most children will, with practice, eventually learn to resist the pull of their devices
when a product is designed to hold attention, expecting children to resist it unaided is unrealistic, so blaming those who fail is unfair
questions.explanation: The analogy stresses a force stronger than individual effort: 'Some will manage. Many will not, and the ones who fail will be told that the failure is theirs.' The point is about unfair expectations and blame, not about rewarding the few who succeed or about swimming itself; nothing suggests most will eventually learn.

relevance.note: Function-of-analogy inference, typical CLAT; distractors clearly off

questions.question: The author's attitude towards proposals to ban children's devices outright is best described as
options: cautiously supportive
sympathetic but sceptical
neutral and uncommitted
dismissive and mocking
questions.explanation: The author calls the instinct 'understandable' (sympathy) but is 'not persuaded', arguing that prohibition treats the symptom as the disease (scepticism). 'Cautiously supportive' overstates agreement; there is no mockery; and the author clearly takes a position.

relevance.note: Tone pairing 'sympathetic but sceptical' vs 'cautiously supportive' — close-adjective trap as in real papers

questions.question: When the author describes boredom as 'less an absence than a threshold', the author means that boredom is
options: a lack of stimulation that ought to be removed as quickly as possible
a sign that a child's surroundings offer too few resources for play
an uncomfortable state that comes just before the mind begins to generate its own ideas
a stage through which children must be carefully guided by adults
questions.explanation: The next sentence explains the image: boredom is 'the discomfort a mind feels just before it is forced to supply its own entertainment'. A threshold is something one crosses, not something to be removed, and the author wants the time to be one that no adult has 'already decided how to fill'.

relevance.note: Figurative-phrase meaning tied to passage's own gloss; fair CLAT item

questions.question: What can most reasonably be inferred from the small circle Haridas draws at the very end of the passage?
options: It marks a hesitation, showing that his habit of noticing what goes unsaid continues even outside the courtroom.
It expresses his relief that he will no longer have to keep records for anyone.
It marks a contradiction in the students' conversation that he intends to point out to them.
It shows that he has decided to retrain as an operator of the new transcription system.
questions.explanation: The passage defines the circle as his mark 'for a hesitation'; he draws it at the moment one student 'nearly apologised and did not'. A contradiction was marked with a slanting line, not a circle, and nothing supports retraining or relief.

relevance.note: Fiction extract inference (CLAT 2024/25 used literary passages); circle=hesitation cleanly supported

questions.question: Justice Varier's remark that accuracy and attentiveness 'are not the same thing' implies that
options: Mr. Menon's transcripts were more accurate than the machine's will be
judges should rely less on written records and more on their own memory of the hearing
the new software is likely to make more spelling mistakes than a human stenographer
a record can reproduce every word correctly and still miss what matters about how those words were said
questions.explanation: She hopes the machine will be 'as accurate' but doubts it will be 'as attentive'; the next line shows the machine spelling 'attentive' correctly while leaving out the smile — accurate words, missed meaning. She does not claim Menon was more accurate, and spelling is exactly what the machine gets right.

relevance.note: Character-remark implication; 'more accurate' distractor is a good partial trap

questions.question: In the sentence 'The screen dutifully printed her words', the word 'dutifully' suggests that the machine acted
options: carefully, choosing each word with precision
reluctantly, and only after a noticeable delay
obediently and mechanically, without any grasp of what it recorded
respectfully, out of a sense of obligation towards the judge
questions.explanation: Used of a machine, 'dutifully' is ironic: it does exactly what it is set to do, printing the words and missing the smile. 'Respectfully, out of obligation' is the word's literal human sense, which a machine cannot have; reluctance and careful choice are not suggested.

relevance.note: Connotation of 'dutifully'; 'respectfully' is a good literal-sense distractor

questions.question: The overall tone of the passage is best described as
options: wistful, with a touch of gentle irony
detached and matter-of-fact
sentimental and openly mournful
bitter and accusatory towards the new technology
questions.explanation: The passage regrets what is being lost (wistful) but is restrained, using quiet irony ('as if that would console him', the machine leaving out the smile). It is not openly mournful or sentimental; Haridas thanks the registrar 'and meant it', so it is not bitter; and it is too clearly sympathetic to be detached.

relevance.note: Tone of narrative; wistful/ironic vs sentimental/mournful close pairing

questions.question: Which of the following would be the most appropriate title for the passage?
options: Thirty-One Years of Punctuality
The Triumph of Courtroom Technology
A Land Dispute in the District Court
What the Transcript Leaves Out
questions.explanation: The story turns on what the machine cannot record — hesitations, gestures, a smile — and on Haridas's habit of noticing them. 'Triumph' misreads the tone; the land dispute and his punctuality are incidental details.

relevance.note: Title question with too-narrow/too-broad distractors per CLAT E02

questions.question: Which of the following best describes Haridas's view of the new transcription system, as the passage presents it?
options: He resents the registrar for having installed it in his place.
He concedes that it is largely competent but notices what it is unable to capture.
He believes it is full of errors and ought to be withdrawn from the court.
He is relieved that it will spare future stenographers years of drudgery.
questions.explanation: 'It did understand, mostly' and it 'caught the advocates' long sentences' show he grants its competence; the following sentences list what it 'did not catch'. He thanks the registrar 'and meant it', so resentment is wrong; nothing suggests withdrawal or relief.

relevance.note: Character-attitude inference; straightforward, slightly easy

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Poorer neighbourhoods are hotter mainly because their residents cannot afford air-conditioning.
Heat action plans have failed to protect the urban poor and should be replaced by large-scale tree planting.
Cities should publish data on every aspect of municipal performance, as they already do for air quality.
Extreme heat falls hardest on poorer neighbourhoods, and cities must move from emergency responses to long-term repair of those areas, helped by making neighbourhood heat measurable.
questions.explanation: The passage moves from unequal heat exposure, through the limits of emergency plans, to long-term repair and the proposal to publish neighbourhood temperatures. Heat plans are credited, not called failures, and trees are 'not only' the answer; lack of cooling is one listed factor, not the cause of higher temperatures; the last option generalises far beyond the passage.

relevance.note: Main idea on policy op-ed; correct option a long composite summary, a bit giveaway

questions.question: The primary purpose of the third paragraph ('Cities have begun to respond …') is to
options: argue that heatwaves are less dangerous than is commonly believed
show that heat action plans have been ineffective in reducing deaths during heatwaves
acknowledge the value of existing measures while arguing that they are designed for a problem whose nature is changing
describe in detail how cooling shelters and changed working hours operate
questions.explanation: The paragraph concedes ('These measures save lives, and they deserve credit') and then pivots ('But they are designed for emergencies … heat … is ceasing to be an emergency'). It does not call them ineffective, gives no operational detail, and does not downplay the danger.

relevance.note: Paragraph-purpose (concede then pivot) — classic CLAT E08

questions.question: The author's observation that shade, 'unlike a flyover, has no ribbon to cut' suggests that
options: projects whose benefits are gradual and unseen win less political support than visible construction
municipal officials are opposed in principle to planting trees
shade-giving measures are too technically complex for municipal bodies to carry out
planting trees costs far less than building flyovers
questions.explanation: Ribbon-cutting is the public ceremony that rewards visible projects; the next sentences say shade's benefits are 'diffuse, slow and invisible' and that budgets rewarding 'visible construction' find it 'a hard sell'. Cost is not compared, no principled opposition is alleged, and the passage says 'None of this is technically difficult'.

relevance.note: Figurative 'no ribbon to cut' meaning; distractors misread the metaphor

questions.question: As used in the passage, the word 'diffuse' most nearly means
options: likely to fade away over time
spread thinly across many people and places
wordy and lacking focus
unclear in meaning
questions.explanation: The benefits are 'diffuse' because they show up scattered across a population as illnesses avoided and working days not lost. 'Wordy and lacking focus' is the sense used of writing, which does not fit benefits; 'fade away' confuses diffuse with temporary.

relevance.note: 'Diffuse' with 'wordy' secondary-sense trap; easy

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely regard as an example of the proposal in the last paragraph working as intended?
options: A city withdraws its heat action plan once it starts publishing neighbourhood temperatures.
A city plants a million saplings in a single monsoon and declares its heat problem solved.
A councillor whose ward routinely records the city's highest summer temperatures is questioned about it once ward-level readings are published.
Residents of treeless settlements are resettled in leafier districts during heatwaves.
questions.explanation: The author argues that published neighbourhood temperatures would 'become a number that councillors could be asked about' — 'what is counted tends to be cared for'. Saplings take a decade to give shade, the author credits heat plans rather than wanting them dropped, and the aim is to repair the neighbourhood, not to move people out of it.

relevance.note: Application of author's proposal to a scenario; well built

questions.question: The tone of the passage is best described as
options: alarmist and fatalistic
urgent but constructive
detached and academic
indignant and accusatory
questions.explanation: The author stresses the danger and the need for change (urgent) but credits existing efforts and offers concrete, achievable remedies (constructive). The passage is not fatalistic ('None of this is technically difficult'), does not blame particular people angrily, and argues for a position rather than simply describing it.

relevance.note: Tone 'urgent but constructive'; distractors fairly distant

questions.question: Which of the following best states the main argument of the passage?
options: Every citizen has a duty to read the statutes that govern him or her.
Laws should be written in everyday conversational language, even if some precision has to be sacrificed.
Lawyers deliberately make statutes obscure in order to protect their professional income.
Much of the obscurity of legal drafting is habit rather than necessity; laws can be made clearer without losing precision, and clarity serves equality before the law.
questions.explanation: The author concedes that precision matters, argues that much obscurity is 'habit', cites redrafting that kept precision, and ties clarity to 'equality before the law'. The author does not accept a loss of precision, never alleges a deliberate income motive, and expressly says not every citizen should be expected to read every statute.

relevance.note: Legal-themed op-ed main idea; extreme distractor 'deliberately obscure' good

questions.question: In the third paragraph, the author primarily
options: concedes part of the lawyers' defence and then argues that it does not justify most legal obscurity
argues that legal drafting should be treated as a form of creative writing
traces the historical origin of the phrase 'notwithstanding anything hereinbefore contained'
rejects entirely the claim that precision matters in legal drafting
questions.explanation: 'There is truth in this' is a concession; 'But the defence proves less than it claims' introduces the counter-argument. The paragraph affirms that drafting 'is not creative writing', does not reject precision, and uses the legal phrase only as an example of habit, not to trace its history.

relevance.note: Paragraph function concede-then-rebut; standard CLAT

questions.question: The author refers to the illustrations attached to provisions of the criminal law in order to
options: argue that criminal statutes are drafted more precisely than tax statutes
prove that clearer drafting reduces the volume of litigation
suggest that courts prefer illustrations to the text of the provision itself
show that Indian law already contains a long-standing and accepted device for making rules easier to understand
questions.explanation: The illustrations are offered as an Indian instance of clarity working ('for more than a century … courts have generally found them helpful'). The passage claims only that redrafting caused no 'measurable rise' in litigation — not a reduction; it does not rank illustrations above the text, and it makes no comparison with tax law.

relevance.note: Purpose of example; 'prove reduces litigation' is an overreach trap

questions.question: With which of the following statements would the author most likely agree?
options: Explanatory notes should replace the operative text of statutes.
Precision in legal drafting is an illusion invented by lawyers.
A small trader who cannot follow a tax notice may become dependent on, and vulnerable to, those who can interpret it.
Obscure laws harm only those citizens who never consult a lawyer.
questions.explanation: The fifth paragraph says such a person 'is placed at the mercy of whoever can' read it. The author accepts that precision matters, proposes notes as aids rather than substitutes, and says the advantage goes to 'those who can afford to have it explained' — implying harm to those who must depend on others, not only to those who never consult anyone.

relevance.note: Author-agree item; correct option near-paraphrase of text, slightly easy

questions.question: The author's attitude towards the lawyers' defence of traditional drafting is best described as
options: partly conceding but ultimately unconvinced
neutral and uncommitted
contemptuous and wholly dismissive
grudgingly persuaded
questions.explanation: The author grants 'There is truth in this' but concludes that 'the defence proves less than it claims'. 'Grudgingly persuaded' reverses the conclusion; the concession rules out 'wholly dismissive'; and the author clearly takes sides.

relevance.note: Attitude 'partly conceding but unconvinced' vs 'grudgingly persuaded' close pair; good

questions.question: Under the Constitution, what is the maximum number of ministers, including the Chief Minister, that the new Tamil Nadu council of ministers may have?
questions.explanation: Article 164(1A), inserted by the 91st Amendment (2003), caps a State council of ministers at 15% of the total strength of the Legislative Assembly (with a minimum of 12). 15% of 234 = 35.1, and since the cap may not be exceeded the maximum is 35. 36 rounds up past the cap; 23 and 47 use 10% and 20%.

relevance.note: Verified TN 2026 result; Art 164(1A) 15% of 234 = 35 with 36/23 rounding traps — strong CLAT GK link

questions.question: The principle that a government's majority must be tested on the floor of the House, rather than decided by the Governor's own assessment, was authoritatively laid down by the Supreme Court in
options: Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006)
S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980)
questions.explanation: The nine-judge bench in S. R. Bommai (1994) held that the floor of the House is the proper forum to test majority, curbing misuse of Article 356. Kesavananda and Minerva Mills concern the basic structure; Rameshwar Prasad (2006) dealt with the dissolution of the Bihar Assembly, not the floor-test rule.

relevance.note: Floor test -> S.R. Bommai; Rameshwar Prasad a credible distractor; event (Vijay floor test May 2026) verified

questions.question: In 1967, the DMK ended Congress rule in the State (then Madras State) and formed its first government. Who became Chief Minister?
options: C. N. Annadurai
M. Karunanidhi
M. G. Ramachandran
K. Kamaraj
questions.explanation: C. N. Annadurai led the DMK to victory in 1967 and became Chief Minister; the State was renamed Tamil Nadu during his tenure. Karunanidhi succeeded him in 1969; Kamaraj was a Congress Chief Minister (1954–63); M. G. Ramachandran founded the AIADMK in 1972.

relevance.note: 1967 Annadurai background fact linked to verified TVK win; standard GK background item

questions.question: Under Article 172, the newly elected West Bengal Legislative Assembly, unless sooner dissolved, continues for five years from
options: the date on which the election results were declared
the date of notification of the general election
the date on which the Chief Minister took the oath
the date appointed for its first meeting
questions.explanation: Article 172(1) fixes the life of a State Legislative Assembly at five years 'from the date appointed for its first meeting' (Article 83(2) says the same for the Lok Sabha). The dates of results, oath or notification are not the starting point.

relevance.note: Art 172 term from first meeting; traps on result/oath date; WB result verified

the Delimitation Commission, under Article 82
the Election Commission of India, under Article 324
the State Election Commission, under Article 243K

Article 3
Article 368
Article 4
questions.explanation: Article 3 empowers Parliament to form new States and alter the areas, boundaries or names of existing States. By a special majority in each House, because it amends the First Schedule
By a special majority in each House and ratification by the legislatures of at least half the States
By a simple majority in each House, because such a law is not deemed an amendment of the Constitution for the purposes of Article 368

prevent customs duty from being charged twice on goods re-exported between the two countries
exempt temporarily posted workers and their employers from paying social security contributions in both countries at once

questions.question: Bilateral and regional free trade agreements such as the CETA and TEPA are a permitted exception, under WTO rules, to which basic principle?

National treatment
Most-favoured-nation treatment
Transparency of trade measures

the European Central Bank
the Council of Europe
the European Parliament

The agreements with EFTA and the UK are in force, while the agreement with the EU has been concluded but has not yet taken effect.
The agreement with the EU is in force, while the EFTA agreement still awaits ratification.
All three agreements — with EFTA, the UK and the EU — are in force.

questions.question: Raghav, a used-car dealer, tells Simran that a car 'has never been in an accident', though he knows it was rebuilt after a serious collision. Relying on this, Simran buys the car. A month later a mechanic tells her the truth. Raghav argues that Simran could easily have had the car inspected before buying. Which of the following is correct?
options: The contract is voidable at Simran's option, because Raghav knowingly asserted a falsehood to induce her to buy, and the 'ordinary diligence' exception does not apply to such fraud.
The contract is voidable only for misrepresentation, because Raghav used no threat or pressure on Simran.
The contract is valid, because Simran had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence by having the car inspected.
The contract is void from the beginning, because any agreement induced by fraud is void.
questions.explanation: Raghav suggested as a fact what he knew to be untrue, intending to induce the sale — fraud under Section 17, making the contract voidable under Section 19. The 'means of discovering the truth' exception is limited to misrepresentation and fraudulent silence, not active false statements. It is not mere misrepresentation (he did not believe it true), and fraud makes a contract voidable, not void.

relevance.note: Fraud vs s19 ordinary-diligence exception — precise principle-application trap, very CLAT

questions.question: Meera sells her house to Arun in May. She knows that the roof leaks badly every monsoon but says nothing about it, and Arun, who inspects the house on a dry day, asks no questions about the roof. Meera and Arun are strangers to each other. After the first rains Arun seeks to avoid the sale. Which of the following is correct?
options: Arun cannot avoid the sale, because a buyer of immovable property always bears the risk of every defect.
Arun cannot avoid the sale, because Meera's mere silence was not fraud: she had no duty to speak and her silence was not equivalent to speech.
Arun can avoid the sale for misrepresentation, because Meera's silence created a false impression that the roof was sound.
Arun can avoid the sale for fraud, because Meera knew a fact that was likely to affect his willingness to buy.
questions.explanation: Section 17 states that mere silence as to facts likely to affect willingness to contract is not fraud unless there is a duty to speak or silence is equivalent to speech; neither applies between strangers where no question was asked. Misrepresentation needs a positive assertion, which Meera did not make. The last option reaches the right result on a rule the passage does not state.

relevance.note: Mere silence not fraud; good misrep/fraud distractors

questions.question: Suppose instead that, before buying, Arun wrote to Meera: 'Unless you tell me otherwise, I shall take it that the roof does not leak.' Meera, who knew of the leak and had recently painted over the damp patches on the ceiling, did not reply. Arun bought the house. Which of the following is correct?
options: Arun cannot avoid the sale, because he could have inspected the house before buying it.
Arun cannot avoid the sale, because mere silence can never amount to fraud.
Arun can avoid the sale, because Meera's silence in these circumstances was equivalent to speech, and the painted-over patches meant the defect could not have been discovered with ordinary diligence.
Arun can avoid the sale, because every seller is under a duty to disclose every defect in the property sold.
questions.explanation: After Arun's letter, Meera's silence was itself equivalent to saying 'the roof does not leak' — fraud by silence under Section 17. Such a contract is not voidable only if the truth could have been discovered with ordinary diligence; the painted-over patches show it could not. The passage recognises no general duty to disclose every defect, and silence can amount to fraud in these circumstances.

relevance.note: Silence equivalent to speech + concealment; follow-up variation as in CLAT sets

questions.question: Kamala, aged 82, is recovering from a stroke and depends on Vinod, her live-in caretaker who also manages her bank accounts. She sells him her flat, worth about ₹1.2 crore, for ₹30 lakh. Later, her daughter brings a suit on her behalf to set the sale aside. Vinod shows that Kamala signed willingly and that he never threatened her. Which of the following is the most accurate statement of the legal position?
options: The sale is valid, because an adult who signs willingly is free to sell her property at any price.
The sale is voidable for coercion, because Kamala was in mental and bodily distress when she signed.
Kamala must prove that Vinod actually pressured her, since there was no threat of any kind.
Vinod must prove that the sale was not induced by undue influence, because he was in a position to dominate Kamala's will and the transaction appears unconscionable.
questions.explanation: Vinod stood in a fiduciary relation to Kamala and contracted with a person whose capacity was affected by age and illness, so he is deemed able to dominate her will; a sale at a quarter of the value appears unconscionable, so Section 16 shifts the burden to him. Coercion requires a forbidden act or threat, which is absent; absence of threats does not answer undue influence.

relevance.note: s16(3) burden shift on unconscionable transaction; coercion trap

questions.question: Kabir tells Dev that he will set fire to Dev's shop unless Dev's sister Nisha sells her plot of land to Farhan, Kabir's friend, at a low price. To protect her brother, Nisha sells the plot to Farhan, who knows nothing of the threat. Can Nisha avoid the contract?
options: Yes, but only if Nisha proves that Farhan obtained an unfair advantage by dominating her will.
Yes, because coercion may be employed by a person who is not a party to the contract and may be directed at someone other than the contracting party.
No, because Farhan, the other party to the contract, neither made the threat nor knew of it.
No, because the threat was directed at Dev's property and not at Nisha herself.
questions.explanation: Threatening to commit mischief by fire is an act forbidden by the criminal law, made with the intention of causing Nisha to enter into the agreement — coercion under Section 15, which applies whoever employs it and whoever is threatened ('to the prejudice of any person whatever'). Domination of will and unfair advantage are elements of undue influence, not coercion.

relevance.note: Coercion by stranger at third party; distractor on innocent party knowledge good

questions.question: An online listing by Tanvi states that her laptop has 16 GB of memory; she honestly believes this but has never checked, and it actually has 8 GB. Rohan, who wants the laptop only for its display, buys it without reading that part of the listing, having told a friend beforehand that he would buy it whatever its memory. He later discovers the truth and seeks to avoid the contract. Which of the following is correct?
options: Rohan can avoid the contract for fraud, because Tanvi had no sufficient grounds for her statement.
Rohan can avoid the contract, because Tanvi's assertion was false and was not warranted by her information.
Rohan cannot avoid the contract, because the misrepresentation did not cause his consent.
Rohan cannot avoid the contract, because Tanvi honestly believed her statement to be true.
questions.explanation: Tanvi's unchecked assertion is a misrepresentation under Section 18 (honest belief does not prevent that), but the passage provides that a misrepresentation which did not cause consent does not make the contract voidable — Rohan never relied on it. It is not fraud, because she believed the statement to be true.

relevance.note: Misrepresentation not causing consent; option B tempting trap

questions.question: A sack of cement falls from a second-floor loading door of Shakti Traders' warehouse and injures Leela, who is walking on the public footpath below. Leela cannot say which of the warehouse workers was careless. Shakti Traders argues that she has failed to prove negligence. Which of the following is correct?
options: Shakti Traders is not liable, because Leela chose to walk past a warehouse where goods were being loaded.
Shakti Traders is not liable, because Leela cannot identify the worker who was negligent.
Shakti Traders is liable whatever explanation it gives, because the sack belonged to it.

Negligence may be inferred, since the sacks were under the control of Shakti Traders' workers and sacks do not ordinarily fall if proper care is used; Shakti Traders must show how it happened without negligence.
questions.explanation: Both conditions of res ipsa loquitur are met, so negligence is inferred without Leela identifying the worker. The inference is rebuttable, so liability is not automatic; walking on a public footpath is not a failure to take care for her own safety.

relevance.note: Res ipsa loquitur (Byrne v Boadle facts) — classic CLAT torts

questions.question: Dr. Iyer performs a knee operation using a technique accepted as proper by a large body of orthopaedic surgeons. A newer technique, preferred by several leading hospitals, would probably have avoided the nerve damage that the patient suffered. Is Dr. Iyer liable in negligence?
options: No, because she acted in accordance with a practice accepted as proper by a reasonable body of surgeons, even though a better method was available.
Yes, because the patient suffered nerve damage that a competent surgeon should have avoided.
No, because doctors cannot be held liable in negligence for their choice of treatment.
Yes, because a better method was available and would probably have avoided the damage.
questions.explanation: Under the Jacob Mathew standard stated in the passage, a professional is not negligent merely because a better alternative was available, provided she followed a practice accepted by a reasonable body of professionals. An adverse outcome is not itself proof of negligence, and professionals are not immune — they are liable if they fall below the ordinary competent standard.

relevance.note: Jacob Mathew/Bolam on accepted practice; better-method trap

questions.question: A cricket ground is surrounded by a five-metre fence. In thirty years, a ball has been hit out of the ground only six times, and no one has ever been hurt. One evening a ball clears the fence and strikes Mohan, who is walking along a quiet residential lane. Mohan sues the club in negligence. Which of the following is the best answer?
options: The club is liable, because it knew that balls had occasionally been hit out of the ground before.
The club is not liable, because the risk was so small that a reasonable person, weighing it, would have been justified in disregarding it.
The club is not liable, because Mohan voluntarily accepted the risk by walking near a cricket ground.
The club is liable, because any harm that is foreseeable must be guarded against.
questions.explanation: The passage says a person need not guard against a risk so small that a reasonable person would think it right to disregard it; six balls in thirty years over a high fence, with no previous injury, is such a risk. Knowledge that something is possible does not create a duty to guard against every foreseeable risk, and walking along a public lane is not consent to the risk.

relevance.note: Bolton v Stone small-risk; volenti distractor

questions.question: Kiran is riding pillion, without a helmet, on a motorcycle that is hit by a speeding bus whose driver was entirely at fault for the collision. Kiran suffers head injuries that would have been much less severe had she worn a helmet. She sues the bus operator. Which of the following is correct?
options: The bus operator is liable, but Kiran's damages will be reduced in proportion to her share of responsibility for her injuries.
The bus operator is not liable, because Kiran failed to take reasonable care for her own safety.
The damages will be halved, because both Kiran and the bus driver were negligent.
Kiran will recover full damages, because her failure to wear a helmet did not cause the collision.
questions.explanation: Contributory negligence concerns the plaintiff's contribution to the damage, not to the accident; not wearing a helmet made her injuries worse. In India this reduces damages in proportion to her share of responsibility — it neither defeats the claim nor automatically halves the award.

relevance.note: Contributory negligence apportionment; 'halved' and 'full damages' traps

questions.question: On her very first day of driving lessons, Farah, trying her best, loses control while turning, mounts the footpath and injures a pedestrian. She argues that she did as well as any beginner could have done. Which of the following is correct?
options: Farah is liable only if she was driving without an instructor beside her.
Farah is not liable, because she did her best and a beginner cannot be expected to do better.
Farah is not liable, because learners are judged by the lower standard of a reasonable learner.
Farah is liable, because the standard of care is that of a reasonable and competent driver, and her inexperience is not taken into account.
questions.explanation: The passage states that the standard is objective and impersonal, and that 'a defendant's inexperience or lack of ability is not taken into account'; she is judged against a reasonable and competent driver. Effort, a separate learner standard or the presence of an instructor are irrelevant on these principles.

relevance.note: Objective standard for learner (Nettleship); reasonable-learner trap

questions.question: A hospital clerk carelessly attaches Ravi's X-ray report to another patient's file. The doctor notices the mix-up before any decision is taken and Ravi's treatment proceeds correctly, without delay. On learning of the error, Ravi sues the hospital in negligence. Which of the following is correct?
options: The hospital is not liable, because it owes patients no duty of care in keeping records.
The hospital is liable, because the clerk's carelessness was a breach of the duty of care owed to Ravi.
The hospital is not liable in negligence, because Ravi suffered no damage as a result of the breach.
The hospital is liable under res ipsa loquitur, because the files were under its control.
questions.explanation: Damage is an essential element: the passage says 'Without damage, there is no actionable negligence, however careless the defendant may have been.' The breach alone is not enough, res ipsa loquitur only helps prove breach, and the hospital does owe a duty — the claim fails on damage.

relevance.note: No damage no negligence; breach-only trap; slightly easy

questions.question: Ravi pledges his gold watch with a licensed pawnbroker as security for a loan of ₹40,000. Before repaying the loan, he slips into the shop one evening and quietly takes the watch back from the display tray without the pawnbroker's knowledge. Which offence, if any, has Ravi committed?
options: No offence, because a person cannot commit theft of property that he himself owns.
Extortion, because he deprived the pawnbroker of the security for his loan.
Theft, because he dishonestly moved the watch out of the possession of the pawnbroker, who lawfully held it, without his consent.
No offence, because he intended to keep the watch only until he could repay the loan.
questions.explanation: The passage states that a person may commit theft of his own property if he dishonestly takes it from another who lawfully holds it; taking the pledge back causes the pawnbroker wrongful loss of his security. A permanent taking is not required, and there is no fear or inducement to deliver, so it is not extortion.

relevance.note: Theft of own property from pawnee — BNS s303 illustration-style, very CLAT

questions.question: A motorcyclist rides close to Geeta as she waits at a bus stop, yanks her handbag from her shoulder and speeds away. Geeta is not touched, hurt or threatened, and realises what has happened only after he has gone. What offence has the motorcyclist committed?
options: Robbery, because he used force to take the bag from her person.
Extortion, because Geeta lost her property against her will.
Theft only, because Geeta suffered no hurt or fear.
Snatching, because in order to commit theft he suddenly and forcibly seized the bag from her possession.
questions.explanation: Grabbing the bag suddenly and forcibly from her possession is exactly what Section 304 calls snatching. Robbery needs hurt, wrongful restraint or fear of instant harm caused to a person — force on the bag alone is not enough. There was no fear and no delivery, so no extortion; 'theft only' ignores the aggravated form created by the BNS.

relevance.note: New BNS snatching offence — topical CLAT 2025-26 point

questions.question: Arjun quietly takes a laptop from a house at night. As he climbs out of the window, the owner wakes, grabs his arm and tries to hold him; Arjun shoves the owner to the floor, bruising him, and escapes with the laptop. Which of the following is correct?
options: Arjun committed robbery, because he voluntarily caused hurt to the owner in order to carry away property obtained by theft.
Arjun committed snatching, because he forcibly took the laptop away from the owner's possession.
Arjun committed extortion, because the owner was put in fear of hurt.
Arjun committed only theft and a separate offence of causing hurt, because the theft was complete before he shoved the owner.
questions.explanation: Section 309 makes theft robbery where hurt is caused 'in carrying away or attempting to carry away property obtained by the theft' and for that end — the shove was to escape with the laptop. The completion of the taking does not prevent this. Nothing was seized from the owner's person, and the owner delivered nothing out of fear.

relevance.note: Theft->robbery when hurt caused in carrying away; 'complete theft' trap

questions.question: In a dark lane, Sameer holds a knife to Tarun's throat and says, 'Hand over your phone.' Terrified, Tarun takes out his phone and gives it to Sameer, who walks away. Which offence has Sameer committed?
options: Snatching, because the phone was taken suddenly from Tarun's possession.
Robbery, because he was present, put Tarun in fear of instant hurt and thereby made him deliver the phone then and there.
Extortion only, because Tarun himself handed over the phone.
Theft, because Tarun did not freely consent to parting with the phone.
questions.explanation: Delivery induced by fear is extortion, and it becomes robbery under Section 309 because Sameer was present, the fear was of instant hurt, and the phone was delivered then and there. It is not theft (property was delivered, not taken without consent) and not snatching (nothing was grabbed).

relevance.note: Extortion as robbery (presence, instant fear, then and there)

questions.question: Meeting Leela at her office, Bhanu tells her that he will have her son beaten up next week unless she transfers ₹1,00,000 to his account. Frightened, Leela makes the transfer two days later from her home. Which of the following is correct?
options: Bhanu committed extortion but not robbery, because the fear was not of instant hurt and the money was not delivered then and there.
Bhanu committed robbery, because he was in Leela's presence when he made the threat.
Bhanu committed theft, because Leela parted with the money without genuine consent.
Bhanu committed no offence, because no one was actually hurt.
questions.explanation: Putting Leela in fear of injury to her son and thereby inducing her to deliver money is extortion. For extortion to become robbery the fear must be of instant death, hurt or restraint and the delivery must be made then and there — here the threat concerned next week and payment came two days later. No actual harm is needed for extortion.

relevance.note: Extortion not robbery — non-instant fear; precise ingredient trap

questions.question: Five friends plan a robbery of a jewellery shop. Four of them enter the shop, threaten the staff with knives and take jewellery, while the fifth waits on a motorcycle just outside the shop, keeping watch and ready to drive them away. Who among them has committed dacoity?
options: Only the four who entered the shop, because the fifth took no property and threatened no one.
Only the fifth friend, because he aided the four who committed the robbery.
All five, because the persons committing the robbery together with the person present and aiding it amount to five.
None of them, because fewer than five persons actually entered the shop and committed the robbery.
questions.explanation: Section 310 counts both those who commit the robbery and 'persons present and aiding such commission'; the look-out waiting just outside to help them escape is present and aiding, making five in all, and every one of them commits dacoity.

relevance.note: Dacoity counting incl. person present and aiding; fits property offences more than claimed L09 joint-liability archetype

questions.question: On Monday, Sunil receives a text message from his neighbour Ajay: 'I will break your legs on Sunday.' On Friday, Sunil goes to Ajay's house and beats him with a stick, so that Ajay will be in no condition to attack him on Sunday. Can Sunil claim the right of private defence?
options: Yes, because a reasonable apprehension of danger had arisen from Ajay's threat, and the right begins as soon as such apprehension arises.
Yes, because he caused only hurt and not death, which is within the limits of the right.
No, because a threat sent by text message is not a threat to commit an offence affecting the human body.
No, because there was ample time to seek the protection of the police, and there was no danger to his body at the time he acted.
questions.explanation: Section 37 denies the right where there is time to have recourse to the public authorities — Sunil had several days. Section 40 ties the right to a present apprehension of danger; a pre-emptive beating days in advance is not defence. The threat was a real threat of an offence against the body; the problem is timing and recourse, not its form.

relevance.note: No PD when time for public authorities / pre-emptive strike; commencement trap

questions.question: Rafiq, who is of unsound mind and incapable of knowing the nature of his acts, suddenly swings an iron rod at Priya's head on a crowded platform. Priya strikes him with a heavy folding chair, breaking his arm. Which of the following is correct?
options: Priya is not protected, because causing grievous hurt always exceeds what is necessary when the attacker is mentally ill.
Priya is protected by the right of private defence, which is available even against a person of unsound mind, and the assault reasonably caused her to fear death or grievous hurt.
Priya is not protected, because Rafiq, being of unsound mind, committed no offence against which private defence could be exercised.
Priya is protected only if she first tried to escape and could not.
questions.explanation: Section 36 expressly extends the right to acts that are not offences only because the doer is of unsound mind. A rod swung at the head reasonably causes apprehension of death or grievous hurt, so even grave harm is within the right (Section 38). The passage imposes no duty to try to escape first.

relevance.note: s36 PD against unsound-mind attacker — direct CLAT principle application

questions.question: Kunal is attacked by Manoj with a knife. Kunal wrestles the knife away, and with the help of passers-by ties Manoj's hands behind his back. While waiting for the police, Kunal, still angry, punches Manoj repeatedly, breaking his nose. Can Kunal claim private defence for the punches?
options: No, because private defence never permits causing grievous hurt to an attacker.
Yes, because Manoj had attacked him with a knife, which reasonably caused fear of grievous hurt.
No, because once Manoj was disarmed and tied up, the danger had ended, and with it the right of private defence.
Yes, because the force used in private defence is not to be weighed in golden scales.
questions.explanation: The right continues only so long as the apprehension of danger continues and is 'not of retaliation or punishment'; a disarmed, tied-up assailant poses no danger. The earlier knife attack would have justified force at that time. The 'golden scales' rule concerns how much force is used during danger, not force after it has ended; grievous hurt can be justified in proper cases.

relevance.note: Right ends with danger; 'golden scales' trap well placed

questions.question: A man rushes at Zoya holding an open bottle, shouting that he will 'burn her face with acid'. Zoya shoves him hard; he falls, hits his head on the kerb and dies. It later turns out that the bottle contained only water. Which of the following is correct?
options: Zoya is protected only because she did not intend to cause the man's death.
Zoya is not protected, because the right of private defence of the body never extends to causing the death of an attacker.
Zoya is not protected, because the bottle contained only water and so there was no real danger.
Zoya is protected, because an attempt to throw what she reasonably believed was acid caused a reasonable apprehension of grievous hurt, and the right then extends to causing death.
questions.explanation: Section 38 extends the right to causing death against an attempt to throw acid that reasonably causes apprehension of grievous hurt; the test is reasonable apprehension, judged as circumstances 'reasonably appeared' to her — what the bottle actually held does not matter. The right can extend to death, and protection does not depend on a lack of intention.

relevance.note: Acid-attack apprehension extends PD to death; reasonable-belief point

questions.question: At night, a farmer sees a fourteen-year-old boy climbing his mango tree and filling a bag with mangoes. Without any warning, the farmer fires his licensed gun at the boy, killing him. The boy was unarmed and had made no threat. Can the farmer claim private defence?
options: Yes, because every person has a right to defend his property against theft.
No, because, although he had a right to defend his property against theft, killing an unarmed boy inflicted far more harm than was necessary for that purpose.
Yes, because the theft took place at night, when he could not seek police help.
No, because the right of private defence is not available against a child.
questions.explanation: The farmer had a right to defend his property against theft, but Section 37 says the right never extends to inflicting more harm than necessary; shooting dead an unarmed boy taking mangoes is grossly excessive. The right is in fact available against children (Section 36), so the last option states a wrong reason.

relevance.note: Excessive harm in property defence; standard

questions.question: A man attacks Anita with a broken glass bottle, slashing at her face. She grabs a heavy wooden stick lying nearby and strikes him once on the arm, fracturing it. At the trial, the prosecution argues that she could have used a lighter stick or simply pushed him away. Which of the following is the best answer?
options: Anita is protected, because she faced a sudden assault that reasonably caused fear of grievous hurt, and her response is not to be weighed in golden scales.
Anita is not protected, because she should have sought the protection of the public authorities.

questions.explanation: Marked price = 8,000 × 1.40 = ₹11,200; selling price = 11,200 × 0.85 = ₹9,520; profit = ₹1,520 = 19% of ₹8,000. Subtracting 15 from 40 gives the trap 25%.

questions.question: During a festival week, the shop gives an additional 5% discount on the already discounted price of the printer. What is the least number of printers it must sell in that week to earn at least as much profit as it earns from selling 10 printers at the normal price?
questions.explanation: Normal profit for 10 printers = 10 × 1,520 = ₹15,200. Festival price = 9,520 × 0.95 = ₹9,044, profit = ₹1,044 per printer. 15,200 ÷ 1,044 ≈ 14.56, so 15 printers are needed (14 earn only ₹14,616).
